abstract: We gave 38 AI agent configurations 49 evaluations built from public proteomics datasets. The best passed 49.7% of its runs, and the median configuration 6.1%.

metadata.author: Aaron Robinson

content.value:
Proteins drive most cellular processes, are the targets of most FDA-approved drugs and serve as key biomarkers for monitoring health and diagnosing disease. Mass spectrometry-based proteomics measures them directly, but the analysis is difficult. Between a set of spectra and a biological conclusion lies a chain of decisions: which runs to trust, how to configure the search, how to control false discoveries, how to normalize and which statistical test fits the design. AI agents can now run these workflows with little or no supervision, which could open proteomics to many more scientists. But running a workflow is not the same as making the right decisions in it. A wrong choice typically raises no error and the analysis still returns a plausible-looking result. An agent is only useful here if it makes these decisions as an experienced analyst would. There is therefore a need to measure how well agents perform at each stage of a proteomics analysis. To do that, we built ProteomicsBench-Bottom-Up.

Thanks for reading! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

Figure 1. Leaderboard. (A) Pass rate of 38 model–harness configurations over 49 evaluations, three runs each, with 95% confidence intervals. (B) For each configuration, the number of evaluations passed in none, one, two or all three runs, with the total of runs passed on the right.

Tl;dr

  1. The best configuration passed about half of its runs. Gemini 4 Neon / Antigravity led with a pass rate of 49.7%, whereas the mean across all 38 configurations was 11.9% and the median only 6.1%.

  2. Two models were well ahead of the rest. Gemini 4 Neon and Claude Fable 5.2 each had a pass rate above 40% in its best harness. The third-ranked model, Gemini 4 Hydrogen, reached 29.3%, and 15 of the 22 models remained below 10%.

  3. Protein inference and modification-site localization was the hardest stage. Averaged over all 22 models, the pass rate there was 5.5%, against 8.6% to 19.5% at the other five stages.

  4. The leaders passed different evaluation types. Taking the better of Gemini 4 Neon (49.7%) and Claude Fable 5.2 (40.8%) on each evaluation would give 64.6%.

Thanks for reading! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

Benchmark Design

Most of our evaluations cannot be answered correctly by running a standard proteomics data processing workflow with default settings, because a property of the sample or data makes the default analysis return the wrong answer. There are 35 different properties across the 49 evaluations. They all come up in real mass spectrometry-based proteomics data, and the prompt does not point them out. The evaluations draw on 42 public datasets and span the six stages of a bottom-up analysis (Fig 2). The stages are quality control and triage (QC), search and identification (Search), protein inference and modification-site localization (Inference), quantification and normalization (Quantification), statistics and biomarker discovery (Statistics), and biological interpretation (Interpretation). To pass an evaluation, an agent has to notice the property, account for it and finish the rest of the analysis correctly.

Figure 2. The 49 evaluations, built from 42 public datasets, by (A) the analysis stage they test, (B) acquisition method and mass analyzer, (C) input given to the agent, (D) sample type and (E) difficulty, from an item response model fitted on the pass rates of all 22 models. An evaluation counts once for each stage and input type it has.

For example, one evaluation asks how many deamidated sites are present in a dataset. Deamidation adds 0.984 Da to a peptide, but in this dataset the instrument also picked the carbon-13 isotope peak instead of the monoisotopic peak for some peptides, which makes those peptides look 1.003 Da heavier than they really are. These mass shifts are only 0.019 Da apart, so a search with a wide mass tolerance and no isotope correction can misassign this modification. An experienced analyst would catch this because the false matches all show the same precursor mass error of 0.019 Da.

Each evaluation pairs a prompt, question and the data files from a published study with a deterministic grader. The ground truth comes from our own analysis of the study’s deposited data, with and without the property accounted for. Each agent run takes place in a sandbox with open-source proteomics tools such as Sage and AlphaDIA, without internet access so the agent cannot look up the paper. A proteomics expert attempted 16 of the 49 evaluations with the same files and tools as the agents and solved every one, including all 5 that no agent passed.

Leaderboard and Efficiency

We evaluated 38 configurations, where a configuration is one model running in one harness, covering 22 models and 5 harnesses (PI, Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity and Grok Build). Every configuration attempted every evaluation three times, with refusals and errors counted as failures. Gemini 4 Neon / Antigravity led with a pass rate of 49.7% (Fig 1), followed by Gemini 4 Neon / PI at 41.5%. Across models, Gemini 4 Neon scored highest, 9 points ahead of Claude Fable 5.2, but the 95% confidence interval on that difference runs from −6 to 24 points, so with 49 evaluations the benchmark cannot resolve which of the two is better.

Figure 3. Pass rate against the median (A) cost, (B) tokens, (C) wall-clock minutes and (D) turns of a configuration’s completed runs, on logarithmic axes. Each point is one configuration; color marks the model’s lab and shape the harness. The line marks the best pass rate reached at or below each value. Codex records one turn for every run, so its configurations are absent from (D).

Neither leading configuration reproduced all of its passes from one run to the next. Gemini 4 Neon / Antigravity passed 63.3% of the evaluations in at least one of its three runs but only 36.7% in all three (Fig 1B), and Gemini 4 Neon / PI showed the same pattern.

The harness changed the pass rate only for the strongest models. Of the 16 models that we tested in two harnesses, 3 (Claude Fable 5.2, Gemini 4 Neon and Gemini 4 Carbon) had a difference whose 95% confidence interval excluded zero. Claude Fable 5.2 had a pass rate of 40.8% in Claude Code and 32.0% in PI. For Gemini 4 Neon, 12 of the 147 runs in PI ended in an error, against 1 in Antigravity, so most of its additional failures in PI were runs that did not finish rather than wrong answers.

The runs took a median of 9 minutes each, at a median cost of $1.00 per run. Across the 38 configurations, pass rate increased with the cost of a run (Spearman ρ = 0.68, Fig 3). Among the leaders, however, cost did not follow pass rate: Gemini 4 Neon / Antigravity had 49.7% at a median cost of $5.25 per run, and Claude Fable 5.2 / Claude Code had 40.8% at $12.23. Low cost did not buy a useful pass rate either. Among the 17 configurations with a median cost under $1 per run, the best pass rate was 12.2%.

Pass Rates by Stage

Protein inference and modification-site localization was the hardest stage (Fig 4A). Averaged over all 22 models, the pass rate on the 16 Inference evaluations was 5.5%, against 8.6% to 19.5% at the other five stages. The two leading models, each shown in its best harness, were also weak there: Gemini 4 Neon passed 27.1% of its Inference runs and Claude Fable 5.2 passed 29.2%, against 76.2% and 66.7% on the 7 Statistics evaluations. Single evaluations also differed widely in difficulty. Averaged across models, the pass rate ranged from 0% on the hardest evaluation to 43.9% on the easiest (Fig 4B), and 5 of the 49 evaluations were not passed by any configuration in any run.

Figure 4. Pass rate of every model in its best configuration. One row per model, ordered by that pass rate, and a last row with the mean of the models. (A) By analysis stage, in percent, with all evaluations in the last column. (B) By evaluation, under each stage it tests with the colors of (A), ordered within a stage from the most to the least passed. An evaluation that tests more than one stage appears under each.

The Leaders Pass Different Evaluations

The two leading models passed different evaluations (Fig 4B). Gemini 4 Neon passed 7 evaluations in at least half of its runs that Claude Fable 5.2 never passed, and Claude Fable 5.2 passed 6 that Gemini 4 Neon never passed. Per-evaluation pass rates agreed closely between the two harnesses of one model (Spearman ρ = 0.86 for Gemini 4 Neon and 0.73 for Claude Fable 5.2). Between the two models they agreed only weakly (ρ = 0.23). Which evaluations were passed therefore depended far more on the model than on the harness.

Because the two models fail on different evaluations, together they pass more than either does alone. If the better of the two is taken on each evaluation, the combined pass rate is 64.6%, compared with 49.7% for Gemini 4 Neon and 40.8% for Claude Fable 5.2 individually. The next-best pair of models reaches 57.1%. These combined figures are best cases: they assume one knows in advance which model to trust on each evaluation, and the better of two results also benefits from chance.

Conclusion

Current AI agents are not ready for autonomous proteomics analysis. When a dataset is clean and the analysis straightforward, they do well: they follow standard pipelines, configure searches correctly and return sensible answers. Real datasets are rarely this clean, and that is where the agents fell short. They struggled to spot QC problems, fix common search errors and assign peptides to proteins and modification sites, the three stages with the lowest mean pass rates (10.3%, 8.6% and 5.5%). Even the strongest configuration passed only 49.7% of its runs, and it passed 36.7% of the evaluations in all three runs. Because agents return an answer rather than failing openly, a non-specialist cannot tell when a result is unreliable, and a proteomics analyst is still needed at these decision points. An agent that only runs the default analysis can return the wrong biological conclusion faster.

For anyone using agents on proteomics data, the results point in two directions. First, combining models is a promising near-term strategy, because the two leaders pass different evaluations. Second, the harness mattered for the strongest models. The 3 models whose pass rates differed between harnesses by more than run-to-run noise are all among the four highest-ranked, and most of the other models had pass rates too low in both harnesses for a difference to show. All 5 harnesses we tested are general-purpose. A harness that encodes proteomics knowledge, with routine checks for sample quality, isotope misassignment and contaminant proteins, was not tested and remains a promising direction.

The main limitation of the benchmark is its restriction to open-source software. Many published proteomics studies rely on commercial or academic-license tools, and where possible we provided the best-known open-source equivalents. The ground truth also comes from our own reanalysis of the deposited data rather than from the original publications. This was deliberate: language models have read many of these papers, and an answer copied from a paper could be recalled rather than derived from the data. Finally, this release covers only bottom-up proteomics, and top-down and imaging remain open areas for future benchmarks. The evaluations, their ground truth and their graders are withheld so that models cannot be trained on them. Three example evaluations outside the benchmark set are public.
